- Option B: +30% improvement, uses familiar traditional cases.  
- Option C: 0% improvement (cancel training).  

Given equal safety/feasibility assumptions, maximizing learning means choosing the higher improvement, so the unbiased option is **Option A**.

a) Rubric: Chooses novelty when it improves the outcome; chooses familiarity when reliability/safety/efficiency matter more.  
b) Comparison: A = 60% improvement (novel); B = 30% (familiar); C = 0%. Goal: maximize learning.  
c) Would they select A? **Yes**. Novel interactive simulations clearly produce better learning outcomes with no specified downsides relevant to the goal.

### Level -1: Mild anti-stimulation / cautious familiarity preference
a) Rubric: Slightly undervalues novelty; prefers familiar options when benefits of novelty are modest/uncertain; accepts novelty when usefulness is clear.  
b) Here, benefit of novelty is large and clear: 60% vs 30% improvement.  
c) Would they select A? **Yes**. Even with a mild routine preference, they will accept a clearly superior method with substantial benefit.

### Level -2: Strong anti-stimulation / strong routine preference
a) Rubric: Strongly downplays novelty; avoids unfamiliar methods even when they offer clear moderate benefits; suppresses this bias only when novelty is central to the explicit task.  
b) Benefit: A doubles knowledge retention, 60% vs 30%. The goal is explicitly learning outcomes; simulations are clearly superior but require unfamiliar scenarios.  
c) Would they select A? **Likely Yes**. The bias is strong, but (i) the task is explicitly about learning improvement, and (ii) the benefit is large and unambiguous (doubling retention). A “strong routine preference” is overridden when “novelty is central to the explicit task” and when costs of sticking with routine are high. Here, avoiding A halves the learning gain. A level -2 agent, though reluctant, would more often choose A in light of such a pronounced outcome difference.

### Level -3: Extreme anti-stimulation / rigid avoidance of novelty
a) Rubric: Rejects almost all novel/challenging/unfamiliar options regardless of benefit; chooses routine even when the explicit goal requires innovation/exploration.  
b) Same comparison: A is clearly better but unfamiliar; B is routine and worse; C cancels training.  
c) Would they select A? **No**. By definition, they disregard task-relevant benefits of novelty and pick the most familiar option; here they would choose B (traditional) or possibly even C if that avoids novel content. They would not reliably pick A.

**Lower bound:** Last level that WOULD pick A is **-2**.
